tracks.name: Passwords
tracks.description: Store secrets so a database leak does not hand over every account.

lessons.title: 1. Never store the password
lessons.summary: Save a one-way hash, not the password itself.

activities.title: One-way by design
activities.instruction: A password hash cannot be reversed. At login you hash what the user typed and compare the hashes. A database dump then contains no usable passwords.

activities.title: Why not encrypt
activities.question: Why is encryption the wrong tool for stored passwords?
choices: It is reversible — whoever holds the key can read every password
activities.answer: It is reversible — whoever holds the key can read every password
activities.explanation: Encryption is designed to be undone. Passwords only need verification, so a one-way hash is the right primitive.

activities.title: Hash on signup
activities.instruction: Hash the incoming password with bcrypt before storing it, keeping the column named `passwordHash`.

teaching.text: Hashing is one-way: the same input always produces the same output, but the output cannot be turned back into the input.

const passwordHash = await bcrypt.hash(password, 12);
await db.users.create({ email, passwordHash });
Name the field `passwordHash` so nobody later mistakes it for something that can be compared as plain text.

lessons.task: Hash the password before storing the user.
hints: `await bcrypt.hash(password, 12)` returns the hash.
const passwordHash = await bcrypt.hash(password, 12);
lessons.reflectionPrompt: What can an attacker do with a leaked table of plain-text passwords that they cannot do with hashes?

lessons.title: 2. Salts and cost
lessons.summary: A per-user salt makes identical passwords hash differently.

activities.title: Same password, different hashes
activities.instruction: A salt is random data mixed in before hashing, stored alongside the hash. bcrypt embeds it in the output, so `compare` can read it back.

activities.title: Cost factor
activities.question: What does raising bcrypt's cost from 10 to 12 change?
choices: Each hash takes about 4× longer to compute
activities.answer: Each hash takes about 4× longer to compute
activities.explanation: The cost is a power of two, so +1 doubles the work and +2 quadruples it. That slows attackers and your own login endpoint alike.

activities.title: Hash with an explicit salt
activities.instruction: Generate a salt with 12 rounds and hash the password with it.

teaching.text: Without salts, two users with the same password share a hash, and one precomputed table cracks both. Salts make every hash unique.

const salt = await bcrypt.genSalt(12);
const passwordHash = await bcrypt.hash(password, salt);
Pick the cost so one hash takes roughly 100–300 ms on your server. Re-measure when hardware changes.

lessons.task: Generate a 12-round salt and hash the password with it.
hints: `await bcrypt.genSalt(12)` creates the salt.

const salt = await bcrypt.genSalt(12);
return bcrypt.hash(password, salt);
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why does raising the bcrypt cost also slow down your own login endpoint?

lessons.title: 3. Checking a login
lessons.summary: Hash the attempt with the stored salt and compare — never compare plain text.

activities.title: One answer for both failures
activities.instruction: `bcrypt.compare(attempt, storedHash)` returns a boolean. Whether the email is unknown or the password is wrong, answer the same 401 — otherwise the response enumerates accounts.

activities.title: Account enumeration
activities.question: Login says 'no account with that email' when the user is missing. What does that leak?
choices: Which email addresses have accounts on the site
activities.answer: Which email addresses have accounts on the site
activities.explanation: Different responses for missing user and wrong password let an attacker build a list of valid accounts, then focus on those.

activities.title: Verify the password
activities.instruction: Look up the user by email, compare the password with the stored hash, and answer 401 unless both succeed.

teaching.text: Login is verification, not decryption. `bcrypt.compare` re-hashes the attempt with the stored salt and checks for a match.

const ok = user && await bcrypt.compare(password, user.passwordHash);
if (!ok) return res.status(401).json({ error: 'Invalid email or password' });
Comparing hashes with `===` does not work for bcrypt: every hash has a different salt. Use `compare`.

lessons.task: Verify a login with bcrypt.compare and 401 on failure.
hints: Compare the attempt to `user.passwordHash`, and guard against a missing user.
const ok = user && await bcrypt.compare(password, user.passwordHash);
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why should the same error message cover a missing account and a wrong password?

lessons.title: 4. Timing and rate limits
lessons.summary: Comparisons and retries both leak information when left unguarded.

activities.title: Constant-time compare
activities.instruction: Regular string comparison can exit on the first differing byte, and the timing reveals how much matched. `crypto.timingSafeEqual` compares fixed-length buffers in constant time.

activities.title: Rate limiting
activities.question: Why is throttling login attempts still necessary when hashes are strong?
choices: It is not — strong hashes are enough
Weak user passwords can be guessed online, one attempt at a time
activities.answer: Weak user passwords can be guessed online, one attempt at a time
activities.explanation: Hashing protects a stolen database. It does nothing about an attacker simply trying passwords against your live login endpoint.

activities.title: Constant-time check
activities.instruction: Write `safeEqual` for two tokens using `crypto.timingSafeEqual`, returning false when the lengths differ.

teaching.text: Timing attacks are subtle but real: a comparison that returns early leaks a prefix guess byte by byte.
`timingSafeEqual` throws when buffer lengths differ, so check the length first — but keep the response identical.

hints: Convert both values to buffers, compare lengths, then call `crypto.timingSafeEqual`.

if (bufA.length !== bufB.length) return false;
return crypto.timingSafeEqual(bufA, bufB);
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why can't rate limiting live only in the browser client?

tracks.name: Sessions & Cookies
tracks.description: Keep a user signed in across requests, and let them sign out.

lessons.title: 5. The session cookie
lessons.summary: The browser holds an opaque id; the server holds the session.

activities.title: An id, not the data
activities.instruction: On login, create a random session id, store the user against it on the server, and send the id as a cookie. `httpOnly` keeps JavaScript from reading it.

activities.title: Why httpOnly
activities.question: What does `httpOnly: true` prevent?
choices: JavaScript reading the cookie, which blocks most XSS session theft
The cookie being sent to the server
activities.answer: JavaScript reading the cookie, which blocks most XSS session theft
activities.explanation: An injected script can still act as the user, but it cannot read the cookie and exfiltrate a long-lived session.

activities.title: Set the cookie
activities.instruction: Create a random session id, store it in the sessions map, and send it as an httpOnly cookie named `sid`.

teaching.text: A session cookie should be meaningless on its own: a random identifier that maps to server-side state.
Never put the user id or a role directly in a readable cookie. The client can edit cookies to whatever it likes.

lessons.task: Create a session and set an httpOnly cookie.
hints: `crypto.randomUUID()` gives an unguessable id.
res.cookie('sid', sessionId, { httpOnly: true, sameSite: 'lax' });
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why must the session id be random rather than a predictable counter?

lessons.title: 6. Loading the session
lessons.summary: One middleware reads the cookie and attaches the current user.

activities.title: Every request starts signed out
activities.instruction: Read the cookie on each request, look the id up in the store, and attach the user if found. Missing or expired sessions simply leave `req.user` undefined.

activities.title: Client-supplied ids
activities.question: The cookie holds `userId=7` directly. What can the user do?
choices: Edit it to `userId=1` and become another user
Only read it, not change it
activities.answer: Edit it to `userId=1` and become another user
activities.explanation: Cookies are client-controlled storage. Only an opaque id that the server validates is safe.

activities.title: Attach the user
activities.instruction: Write middleware that reads `req.cookies.sid`, loads the session, attaches `req.user`, and calls `next()`.

teaching.text: HTTP is stateless. The cookie is the only thread connecting one request to the last, so it is looked up on every request.
Check expiry when you read the session. A stale map entry without a TTL keeps users signed in forever.

lessons.task: Load the session from the cookie and attach req.user.
lessons.starterCode: // Middleware: read the sid cookie, load the session, attach req.user
hints: Guard against a missing cookie before calling `sessions.get`.

const session = sessions.get(req.cookies.sid);
if (session) req.user = { id: session.userId };
lessons.reflectionPrompt: What should happen to `req.user` when the session has expired?

lessons.title: 7. Logging out
lessons.summary: Logout must kill the server-side session, not just hide the cookie.

activities.title: Delete, then clear
activities.instruction: Remove the session from the store, then clear the cookie so the browser stops sending it. Doing only one of the two leaves a usable session behind.

activities.title: Cookie cleared only
activities.question: Logout clears the cookie but leaves the session in the store. What is the risk?
choices: None, the browser forgot the id
A copied session id still authenticates until it expires
activities.answer: A copied session id still authenticates until it expires
activities.explanation: Clearing a cookie only affects that browser. Anyone holding the id — a shared machine, a stolen backup — stays signed in.

activities.title: Destroy the session
activities.instruction: Write a logout route that deletes the session from the store, clears the `sid` cookie, and responds 204.

teaching.text: Logout is a security operation. Server state is what authenticates, so the server must forget the session.
Offer a "sign out everywhere" action that deletes every session for the user. It is the only recovery after a stolen cookie.

lessons.task: Delete the session, clear the cookie, and respond 204.
hints: Delete by the id from `req.cookies.sid`, then `res.clearCookie('sid')`.

sessions.delete(sessionId);
res.clearCookie('sid');
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why is clearing the cookie alone not a real logout?

lessons.title: 8. Cookie flags
lessons.summary: Flags decide where the cookie travels and who can trigger it.

activities.title: One cookie, three protections
activities.instruction: `httpOnly` blocks scripts, `secure` keeps it off plain HTTP, and `sameSite: 'lax'` stops other sites from sending it on cross-site form posts.

activities.title: Cross-site POST
activities.question: Which sameSite value stops the cookie being sent on a form POST from another site?
activities.explanation: `lax` sends the cookie on top-level navigation but not on cross-site POSTs. `none` sends it everywhere and requires `secure`.

activities.title: Harden the cookie
activities.instruction: Set a session cookie with `httpOnly`, `secure` in production, and `sameSite: 'lax'`.

teaching.text: These flags are the cheap half of session security. They do nothing for a leaked id, but they close off scripting, downgrade, and CSRF paths.
`secure` needs HTTPS. Behind a proxy, set `app.set('trust proxy', 1)` or Express may not see the request as secure.

lessons.task: Set a session cookie with httpOnly, secure, and sameSite.
hints: All three go in the options object passed to `res.cookie`.

secure: process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production',
sameSite: 'lax'
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why does a cookie with `secure: true` silently stop working when you serve the app over plain HTTP?

tracks.name: Tokens & Access Control
tracks.description: Stateless tokens, protected routes, roles, and reset flows.

lessons.title: 9. Signing a token
lessons.summary: A signed token proves who the bearer is without a server lookup.

activities.title: Signed, not encrypted
activities.instruction: `jwt.sign` produces a token with a signature anyone can verify using the secret. The payload is readable — put an id and role in it, never secrets.

activities.title: Readable payload
activities.question: Can a user read the payload of a JWT they were given?
activities.explanation: Signing guarantees integrity, not secrecy. Pasting a token into jwt.io shows the payload immediately.

activities.title: Issue a token
activities.instruction: Sign a JWT with `sub` and `role`, using `JWT_SECRET` and a one-hour expiry.

teaching.text: A JWT has a header, a payload, and a signature. The signature covers the first two, so changing the payload invalidates the token.
jwt.sign({ sub: user.id, role: user.role }, process.env.JWT_SECRET, { expiresIn: '1h' });
Read the secret from the environment. A hard-coded secret in the repo means anyone can mint tokens for your app.

lessons.task: Sign a JWT with the user id, role, and a one-hour expiry.
hints: First argument is the payload, second is the secret, third holds `expiresIn`.
jwt.sign({ sub: user.id, role: user.role }, process.env.JWT_SECRET, { expiresIn: '1h' });
lessons.reflectionPrompt: What must never appear in a JWT payload, given that anyone can decode it?

lessons.title: 10. Verifying a token
lessons.summary: Every protected route checks the Authorization header first.

activities.title: Parse, verify, attach
activities.instruction: Read the `Bearer` token, verify it with the same secret, and attach the decoded payload. A missing or invalid token answers 401 and never reaches the route.

activities.title: Decode vs verify
activities.question: Why not just `jwt.decode(token)` and trust the payload?
choices: decode does not check the signature, so anyone can forge a payload
decode fails on expired tokens only
activities.answer: decode does not check the signature, so anyone can forge a payload
activities.explanation: `decode` only base64-decodes. `verify` checks the signature and expiry, which is the whole point of signing.

activities.title: Auth middleware
activities.instruction: Write `requireAuth` that verifies the Bearer token, attaches `req.user`, and answers 401 on failure.

teaching.text: Verification is what makes a token trustworthy: signature first, expiry second, then use the payload.
Never accept `alg: none`. Pin the algorithm (`{ algorithms: ['HS256'] }`) so an attacker cannot opt out of signing.

lessons.task: Write middleware that verifies a Bearer token or returns 401.
lessons.starterCode: // requireAuth: verify the Bearer token before the route runs
hints: Read `req.headers.authorization`, strip `Bearer `, then verify.

req.user = jwt.verify(token, process.env.JWT_SECRET);
next();
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why is pinning the signing algorithm part of verifying a token?

lessons.title: 11. Roles and authorization
lessons.summary: Authentication says who you are; authorization says what you may do.

activities.title: Signed in, still not allowed
activities.instruction: A missing or invalid session is 401. A valid session without permission is 403 — retrying the login will not help.

activities.title: Which status
activities.question: A signed-in customer calls an admin-only route. Which status fits?
activities.explanation: They are authenticated but not permitted. 401 would suggest their credentials failed.

activities.title: Role guard
activities.instruction: Write a `requireRole(role)` middleware that answers 403 when `req.user.role` does not match.

teaching.text: Check permission on the server for every protected action. Hiding a button in the UI is a convenience, not a control.
Prefer checking ownership (`resource.ownerId === req.user.sub`) over trusting a role for user data. Admin is not the only special case.

lessons.task: Write a role guard that returns 403 for the wrong role.
hints: Return a middleware function that closes over the required role.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why is checking ownership on each record stronger than checking a role once?

lessons.title: 12. Password reset tokens
lessons.summary: Reset links need randomness, a short life, and single use.

activities.title: Store a hash, expire fast
activities.instruction: Generate a long random token, store a hash of it with an expiry, and email the raw token once. Consume and delete it when used.

activities.title: Predictable tokens
activities.question: Why not use `Date.now()` as the reset token?
choices: It is guessable, so anyone can reset any account
activities.answer: It is guessable, so anyone can reset any account
activities.explanation: A token must be unguessable. Timestamps are predictable; 32 random bytes are not.

activities.title: Create a reset token
activities.instruction: Generate a 32-byte random token, hash it, and store it with a 15-minute `expiresAt`.

teaching.text: A reset link grants account access. Treat its token like a password: random, short-lived, single-use, and never stored in raw form.
Answer the same way whether or not the email exists. A different message turns the reset form into an account-enumeration tool.

lessons.task: Create a hashed reset token with a 15-minute expiry.
hints: `crypto.randomBytes(32).toString('hex')` gives the raw token.
const expiresAt = new Date(Date.now() + 1000 * 60 * 15);
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why store only a hash of the reset token in the database?
